what: The lane state is a tea machine, but an LLM operator sits on top deciding each next step and waiting for CI. An operator run that only waited for CI and passed the PR to a reviewer cost about 110k-120k tokens.
cause: fabrika's operate skill puts the drive loop in a prompt; the machine only records what the agent reports.
fix: The machine picks the next step itself. Waiting for CI is a Listen (CI reports back on its own), so no agent waits.
test: Sum operator tokens in runs.jsonl against builder and reviewer tokens per lane; run the same lane under tea-fabrika and compare.

what: A builder stopped on a decision ticket because the ruling answered one of three asks. It recorded BLOCKED with no cause. With no cause, the park can only be cleared by a person, so the whole epic waited.
cause: fabrika 0.9.0 has no park cause for 'ruling owed'; a builder's stop is free text plus a token, not a typed answer.
fix: The builder's stop is a typed value with a required cause (e.g. ruling-incomplete, naming the missing asks). A stop with no cause can't be built.
test: Count parks with no cause in runs.jsonl over time; zero once the answer is typed.

what: The ruling posted on a decision ticket answered the bump per tier but not the two other asks in the same criterion (changelog callout per tier, and whether the policy doc gains a sentence). The lane was unblocked on it anyway and a builder found the gap later.
cause: Nothing compares a ruling with the criterion it is meant to settle before the lane moves on.
fix: Before an unblock, check the ruling against each ask in the criterion: code splits the asks, a narrow Judge answers 'does this ruling answer ask N?' per ask. A miss goes back to the person at once, not after a builder spends a run.
test: Replay: decision tickets with rulings; count rulings that would have been sent back.

what: Epic children run in phases. #609 doesn't depend on #612, but #612 is in phase 1, so #609 can't start while #612 is parked. Moving it means re-planning the epic.
cause: The plan is a list of phases, not the real dependency edges.
fix: The parent is written by hand with real edges, so a child starts when its own inputs are ready.
test: Per epic, compare wall time under phases with wall time under the dependency graph.

what: The epic's plan approval went stale after a ruling on one child changed that child's labels, and had to be given again.
cause: Approval is checked against a snapshot of labels, so any later label change reads as a changed plan.
fix: The approval is an event in the epic's own log, bound to the plan's content, not to label snapshots.
test: Count re-approvals per epic.

what: The skills tell the operator to run lane worktree, lane cleanup and lane leave; the installed CLI (0.9.0) has none of them. Every run skipped them, and agent working copies piled up on disk.
cause: Skill text and CLI ship separately and drifted.
fix: Cleanup is an Act in code that ships with the machine, run when the lane ends. No prose step to skip.
test: Count leftover working copies after a day of lanes.

what: A plugin reload dropped every fabrika agent type from the session. Two operators stopped mid-lane because they could no longer spawn a reviewer, and the lanes waited until the plugin loaded again.
cause: The marketplace source in the user settings (a local folder) didn't match the installed marketplace (GitHub), so the plugin was ignored on reload.
fix: Roles are code the machine calls, not agent types loaded from config at run time. A config problem fails at start, not mid-lane.
test: Count lanes stopped by tooling, not by the work.

what: Another PR merged first, so the lane's PR conflicted while in review. The machine had no step for 'base conflicted' in review and refused the report. The operator parked itself, ran a repair builder, and cleared its own park by hand.
cause: fabrika 0.9.0's review state has no arm for a base conflict.
fix: A base change is something the lane listens for; a conflict while in review goes to repair as a normal step.
test: Count conflicts handled by hand in runs.jsonl.

what: build check is red on every lane because of one guard (codeowners-cp) that doesn't apply to this repo. Every builder and every operator brief has to say 'ignore this one'.
cause: The guard reads a CODEOWNERS shape meant for another repo.
fix: A check that is always red teaches agents to ignore red. Checks are per repo, in settings, and one that can't apply is off.
test: Count briefs that carry an 'ignore this red' line.

what: An operator was asked to report before its reviewer finished. It stopped, and the reviewer ended its turn while waiting on CI, so neither was driving and a new operator had to be started to carry on.
cause: A child agent's life is tied to its parent's turn, not to the lane.
fix: The wait belongs to the machine; a child that waits is a Sub the machine owns, so stopping the driver doesn't drop it.
test: Count lanes where a child was left with no parent.

what: The driver merged a ROADMAP PR by hand with gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch on a repo with a merge queue. The merge failed, and --delete-branch closed the PR; it had to be reopened.
cause: A world-changing step was open to the driver instead of only to the shipper.
fix: Merge is an Act only the machine can take, through the queue. The driver has no merge verb.
test: Count merges not made by the shipper.

what: A criterion lists 8 files from a grep for a name; 2 of them mention the name only in comments. The builder noticed the list is wrong, but only a person can fix the ticket.
cause: The criterion's file set was written from text search, not from what the code uses.
fix: Code facts (code-graph) gather where a name is used, and vetting checks every file a criterion names before the ticket is ready.
test: Replay: count criteria whose file sets disagree with code-graph.

what: A gap report was filed and then closed the same day as working as designed: the spec already says abstract methods aren't nodes.
cause: The report was written before reading the spec section it touched.
fix: Before a report is filed, gather the spec and doc pages that name the thing (facts read the doc pages a ticket names), and show the reporter any that already answer it.
test: Count reports closed as by-design.

what: The triager corrected the brief it was given: the brief said #609 builds on the function #616 changes; reading #609 showed it doesn't. It wrote the correction as a note instead of acting on the wrong claim.
cause: The triager read the source instead of trusting the brief.
fix: Keep it: claims in a brief are checked against the source before they shape a ticket.
test: Count brief claims a stage corrected.

what: The reviewer built the base and the head, ran the ticket's exact fixture twice on the head (byte-identical), and compared hashes of the whole package's output on base and head to show nothing else moved.
fix: Make this the default check: run the fixture on head twice and base once, and diff the whole package's output.
test: Replay: does a base/head output diff catch the extra changes found by hand in past reviews?

what: After a ruling, the unblock had to be typed by hand from the main checkout (decision rule, then lane transition). Running the transition twice was refused the second time with an engine error, not a 'already done' answer.
cause: The unblock is a separate hand step and the transition isn't idempotent.
fix: ask = Act + Listen: the lane posts the question and listens for the ruling; when it lands and passes the check (note 03), the lane moves on by itself.
test: Count hand transitions per ruling.

what: Three sibling issues were triaged in parallel and gave three different answers to the same question, where they live. One parked and asked the owner; two put themselves on an existing milestone at p1. The owner then chose a new campaign, so all three had to be moved again, partly by hand.
cause: Each triager judged the home alone; nothing shared one answer across the batch.
fix: A question that several tickets share is asked once for the batch. Every sibling listens for that one answer instead of guessing its own.
test: Count batches where siblings got different homes, then a re-home.

what: Claim markers left by finished triage runs held the issues for about 50 minutes. A re-home triager sat waiting for them and was stopped (the driver moved the milestones by hand). The run that finished #599's triage took 25 minutes, most of it waiting for a sibling claim to expire.
fix: Who holds a lane is lane state, released when the run ends, not a timed marker that outlives it.
test: Sum minutes runs spend waiting on claims in runs.jsonl.

what: Three triagers in parallel each ran npx to get the same code-graph build. One failed on the shared npx cache (ENOTEMPTY) and had to install its own copy.
fix: Code facts are gathered once by code and handed to every run, so parallel agents don't each fetch the same tool.
test: Count runs that fetch a tool another run already fetched.

what: The driver started a shipper without its own working copy. The ship verb refused at once (exit 33) and the shipper read nothing. It also had no review verdicts to ship on. This is the run right before the hand merge in note 11.
cause: The ship verb refuses to run from the main checkout, and the driver's spawn didn't ask for a separate copy.
fix: The machine starts each role with the setup that role needs (its own copy, verdicts in place). The driver can't start a shipper wrong.
test: Count role runs refused for setup, not for the work.

what: The driver started separate operators on two children of an epic. The #612 operator stopped at once: a child can't get a lane while its epic has none (lane open exit 48). The driver stopped the #608 one and started a single operator on the epic.
cause: Epic children only run inside the epic's lane; the driver didn't know that when it spawned them.
fix: The machine decides what runs next from the epic's own state. There is no driver choosing which ticket gets an operator.
test: Count operators stopped because they were started on the wrong ticket.

what: The epic plan says child #609 needs #601, which is not a child of the epic. Starting the epic lane refused on that (exit 16). The operator restarted it with a flag that drops the edge, then checked by hand that the epic branch already held #601's commit.
cause: The lane machine only knows edges between the epic's own children.
fix: The parent is written with real edges, including edges to work outside the epic; the lane listens for that outside ticket to land.
test: Count plan edges dropped or checked by hand.

what: The owner's ruling on decision child #612 was already a comment, but the first builder couldn't see it: claim refused the decision ticket (exit 30) because no ruling had been recorded with a separate command, and the builder had no verb to read the thread. The lane parked with no cause. The operator then recorded the ruling, but the park still needed a person to clear it.
cause: A ruling only counts once a second command stamps it; the comment itself is not an event the lane sees.
fix: The ruling comment is the event. The lane listens on the ticket, so a posted ruling reaches it without a stamping step.
test: Count builder runs spent on decision tickets before their ruling was recorded.

what: Two triagers gave different shapes for the pitch approval line. One said it must carry a UTC timestamp and that an agent must never post it; the other said there is no timestamp and the line is the whole grammar. The approvals were then posted in both shapes.
fix: An approval is a typed event with one schema, checked when it lands, so no agent has to describe the grammar.
test: Count approvals rejected or re-posted for shape.

what: A reviewer's non-blocking note (abstract-method overloads missing from headers) was filed as #615. Its triager built the code and ran a test file: abstract methods aren't nodes at all, by the spec, so there was nothing to fix. The note had come from reading the code, not running it.
cause: The triager found the note was written from reading one function; no fixture backed it.
fix: A review note only becomes a follow-up after a small fixture shows the gap. A note with no run behind it stays a note.
test: Count follow-ups from review notes closed as by-design.

what: Two lanes went from triaged to merged with no person and no repair: one build, one review, one ship each, about 31-34 minutes. Token split per lane: operator 27% and 32%, builder 42% and 34%, reviewer 23% and 24%, shipper 8% and 10% (437k and 373k tokens in all).
fix: The happy path works; the operator's quarter to a third of the spend is the part machine-drives would remove.
test: Run the same kind of lane under tea-fabrika and compare the total against these two.

what: Where lane leave did exist, it still couldn't clean up: it exited 74 because the agent's own working copy is locked by the harness while that agent is running.
cause: The error says the working tree is locked by the running agent.
fix: Cleanup is an Act the machine runs after the agent has ended, not a step the agent runs on itself.
test: Count working copies left after lanes end.

what: Four lanes in the same package ran at once. #599's PR conflicted twice as the others merged first: once in review, once at ship. Each time it went back to a builder, then CI, then a fresh review, before it could land. Both conflicts were in the same spec section, and both were resolved by keeping both sides.
cause: Parallel lanes in one package edit the same shared doc; nothing orders them or merges the doc mechanically.
fix: The lane listens for main moving; a conflict in a doc both sides only append to goes to a cheap code merge or a narrow repair, not a full build-review cycle. Lanes that touch the same spec section are ordered by the parent.
test: Per lane, count rebuild-and-review cycles caused only by a base move.

what: An operator's first turn already holds about 88k tokens, before it reads the lane: the operate skill is 2,556 lines. A run that made 9 tool calls still reported 104k. Most of what an operator costs is being told how to operate.
cause: Read from the operator transcripts: the context size at the first turn of two short runs.
fix: The routing table, the park causes and the recipes are code (src/fabrika.ts). Nothing reads the skill, so that starting cost is gone, not shrunk.
test: Experiment 48: the machine's row in runs.jsonl is 0 tokens; compare a lane's total against #600 and #601.

what: Across the day's 13 operator runs, about 132 next-step choices, counted by hand. About 88 were routing by state name. 44 were not; 20 of those were the agent working around its setup (no CLI in its working copy, verbs the CLI lacks). Of the 24 real judgment calls, a code rule decides 14, one narrow Jev question fits 9, and 1 needed a person.
cause: Counted from the transcripts' commands and the text around the non-routine steps; the totals are rough, the 17 kinds of call are exact.
fix: The 14 are rules in the operator machine or in the Fabrika service's typed answers; the 9 are named Judge questions, not built yet; the 1 is an ask.
test: Experiment 48's step-0 table: rerun the count on a later day and see which rows are gone.

what: 7 of 13 operator runs stopped short of the lane's end. Three were the driver's doing, two lost their agent types to a plugin reload, and two parked for a person. Only one of those two needed a person: the other waited on a ruling that was already recorded, because the park had no cause and the recipe will not clear a park with none.
cause: The park was a bare BLOCKED; recipe unpark refuses one at exit 12.
fix: A park always carries a typed cause. A ruling-owed park clears by a recipe once a ruling newer than the park stands; only a ruling that leaves a question open goes to ask.
test: Count parks that reached a person, and how many of them a person had already answered.

what: One epic operator carried five children from build to landed on the epic branch in one run of about 131 minutes, each with its own review, then assembled one green PR. It stopped once, at the right place: the PR changes a protected workflow file and no owner had approved it. The park has a typed cause, and the shells filed five follow-up issues on the way.
fix: Keep it: a protected path is a gate with a typed cause that only a named person can pass. The machine can know this stop is coming from the plan (one child touches a protected file) and ask for the approval while the other children build, instead of at the end.
test: Per epic, time from last child landed to merged; compare asking at plan time with asking at ship time.

what: A lane ran from claim to merged with no operator agent. tea-fabrika's operator machine claimed it, made one working copy, ran a builder, waited 7 minutes on CI, ran a reviewer and a shipper, posted the record, removed the copy and released the lane, in 18.8 minutes. Its own spend was 22 Cmds and 60 fabrika verbs: no tokens, no Jev call, no person. The three shells cost $1.74.
fix: Keep it. The operator's 116k to 119k tokens on a clean lane are gone; the shells are unchanged.
test: Run it on a code issue that takes a repair round, and on two lanes at once, before calling it a rate.

what: A wiring check claimed a real issue. A builder shell started through the Agent SDK as the main agent had no skill in its context, called the Skill tool, and the build skill (declared to run as a second agent in the background) picked the next ready issue, claimed #593, read it, and released the claim. Nothing was left on the issue.
cause: Checked in the dry run's log: an agent definition's preloaded skills only reach a subagent spawn, not an SDK session's main agent.
fix: The host puts the shell's skill in front of its brief in code, the Check refuses the Skill tool for a skill already loaded, and a dry run gets read-only tools.
test: The preload and runner dry runs: the shell quotes its skill back with no tool call, and ends with a typed last word.

what: The shipper still ran lane cleanup, a verb the installed CLI does not have, got exit 1, and told the person the lane's working copies were left on disk. They were not: the machine removed its one copy four seconds after the lane's record was posted.
cause: The skill is newer than the pinned CLI (0.9.0), and it still owns a cleanup step the machine now does.
fix: Take cleanup out of the shells' skills when a machine drives: the copy is the machine's from make to remove. Until then the shell's closing words about leftover copies are wrong and should not reach a person.
test: git worktree list before and after a lane; count shell closings that mention leftover copies.

what: Two things broke the typed last word before any lane ran. The SDK refused the answer's JSON Schema because of the $schema line zod adds, and the run died before its first turn. With that fixed, a named agent with its own tool list never got the SDK's answer tool, so its answer came back empty.
cause: Both seen in the runner dry run.
fix: The schema is sent without $schema. When the SDK hands back no structured answer, code reads the last JSON object in the shell's closing text that fits the schema; anything else is null, never text.
test: On #559 all three shells' last words parsed: SHIPPED-PR, PASS, LANDED. None was needed, because each shell's own report landed.

what: Where the 18.8 minutes went: 11.1 in the three shells, 7 waiting for CI before review, under 1 in the machine. The shipper's 6.5 minutes were almost all its own wait on checks and the merge queue, with an opus session held open and idle.
cause: Read from the run's log: the times of each Cmd, each shell's start and end.
fix: The wait before review is already a Listen and cost nothing. The shipper's waits could be Listens too: a Check for its gates, an Act to enqueue, a Listen on the queue, and no agent.
test: Ship one lane with the gates as code and compare the 6.5 minutes and $0.30.

what: Five sibling issues were triaged in parallel, each told its home up front (milestone 7). All five agreed, and none waited on another: 2.1 to 3.1 minutes and 72k to 81k tokens each. The morning before, three siblings given no home gave three different answers (note 2026-10-10-17).
cause: The one fact that differed between the two batches was the home, handed in with the task instead of left for each triager to work out.
fix: Keep it. A fact siblings share is gathered once, before they start, and handed to each as data. Nothing a parallel agent has to guess should be something its parent already knows.
test: Per triage batch, count siblings whose home differs from the batch's and how many had to be moved after.

what: A lane failed its first review and was repaired with no operator agent and no person. The first PR's required check went red on CI (a second stderr line that only shows on Linux). The machine saw the checks settle, started the reviewer, the reviewer read the failing log and failed both verdicts, the lane went back to build, a builder found and fixed the cause, the second review passed, and the PR merged through the queue. 40.2 minutes, $7.68, 49 Cmds, no tokens of the machine's own.
fix: Keep it. The repair loop needed no new code: review's FAIL folds the lane back to build, and the routing table sends build to a builder whatever round it is.
test: Run more lanes that fail review; this is one.

what: Three builders in a row were recorded dead though each had finished its work. Each pushed or checked the repair, started its wait on CI as a background command, and ended its turn to wait. Under the machine a shell is the one agent of a one-shot session, so the session ended there, with no report to the lane. The machine recorded a dead shell and started the next builder, which did the same, until CI finished and the fifth one could report. The three extra builders cost $1.94, a quarter of the lane.
cause: Read in the shells' transcripts: run_in_background true on the CI wait, then the turn ends. A Claude Code subagent is woken when a background command finishes; an SDK session's main agent is not.
fix: Now: the Check refuses a background command and the shell is told why. Better: the builder should not wait on CI at all. The machine already listens to the PR's checks before review, for free. And a shell that ends with no report should be asked to finish in its own conversation, not replaced by a new one that reads everything again.
test: Count dead-shell laps per lane, and how many of those shells had pushed work.

what: The Check before each shell step refused two harmless commands: one redirecting to /dev/null inside a subshell, one to /dev/stdout. It read both as writes outside the working copy. The builder reworded each and went on.
cause: The path rule took a closing bracket as part of the path, and knew /dev/null but no other device.
fix: Fixed: a path loses what closes a subshell, and anything under /dev is no file. A Check that refuses what is fine teaches a shell to route around it, which is the opposite of its job.
test: Per lane, count refusals and how many were right. On #625: 2 refusals, 0 right.

what: The first reviewer was started on a PR whose required check was already red. It spent $1.00 and 2.2 minutes, and its finding was the CI failure, read from the log, with a likely cause. The machine knew the checks were red before it started the reviewer.
cause: The machine waits for checks to settle, green or red, then briefs the reviewer either way.
fix: Not decided. A gate could send a red PR straight back to the builder with the failing job's log, and skip the reviewer. But this reviewer's note (the fix belongs in the product, not in a looser test) is the kind of steer a log does not carry.
test: On lanes whose first review fails on red CI, compare the repair with and without the reviewer's note.

what: Before a review, four operator runs read the PR's checks as still running. Three started the reviewer anyway (the tail PR of #604, #605, and #616, where the merge state was also unknown after three reads). One waited (#599). The skill says wait. Given the same tool output, Jev and Opus both answered wait all four times.
cause: Read in the operator transcripts: the build verdicts output and the command after it. Nothing in the lane stops a reviewer from starting on checks that have not settled, so it is left to each operator.
fix: Already in the machine: the review turn listens until the checks settle, as a rule in code. No Judge is needed for it, and agreeing with a rule is no reason to pay for a call.
test: experiment 51, the gate cases: Jev matched Opus on the same text 7 of 7 and matched the operators 2 of 5.

what: A lane parked on purpose, and tea-fabrika's operator machine asked a person for the first time. The pull request changes a file under /.github/, which has owners. Fabrika's shipper found no owner approval on the head, noted it on the PR, and parked the lane at human:cp-approval. The machine tried fabrika's recipe once (not yet), posted one question on the issue, listened for 10 minutes, heard nothing, and ended parked: working copy removed, lane released, question left on the issue, PR open and untouched. 28.3 minutes, $3.22, 23 Cmds, no Jev call.
fix: Keep it. The unanswered ending is what lets a 12-hour wait cost nothing: no process, no claim and no working copy are held while a person is away.
test: Park more lanes and count how each ends: answered inside the wait, parked, or cleared by a later run.

what: Caught before the run, by reading fabrika's source: a second run would have read its own claim as the owner's reply. Fabrika 0.9.0 posts a lane's claim on the issue as a plain line (lane-claim: ...) with no hidden mark, under the account the owner replies from. The second run claims the lane after the first run's question was posted, so the claim is a later comment by a listed person. On a made-up claim line the Judge answered leave at 0.46, under the floor, so it would have been set aside at the cost of one call.
cause: The thread Layer took every comment without a hidden mark for a person's. Fabrika's claims, build claims, adoptions and lane records carry none. The scripted fake's thread has no claims on it, so no test could see this.
fix: Fixed: the thread Layer knows fabrika's unmarked records by their keyword, and now has tests of its own over a stand-in gh. It is a list of keywords from one CLI version, so it goes stale when fabrika adds a record.
test: On a lane's second run with the recipe still saying not yet, count Jev calls against replies a person wrote. They should match.

what: The machine's first question to a person did not say what to do. It named the park (human:cp-approval, awaiting-cp-approval) and three choices. It did not name the pull request or say that an owner has to approve it. The shipper's note on the PR said so; the issue, where the person was asked, did not.
cause: The question was built from the state's name and the cause only. The pull request was in the turn's state the whole time.
fix: Fixed after the run: the question names the pull request whenever the lane has one, and for an approval park says to approve it, who may, and to answer /resume after.
test: Give the question to someone who has not seen the lane and ask what they would do next.

what: The person's reply was never read. The second run tries the park's recipe before it looks for its question. The approval was in, so fabrika's recipe cleared the park 15 seconds into the run and the lane went on to ship. The person had been asked for two things, an approval and a reply, and only the approval counted. Read offline, the Judge took the reply as resume at 1.00. Also: once a question is posted the machine never tries the recipe again in that run, so an approval given inside the wait would not have been seen until the wait ran out and someone started another run.
cause: gatePark tries the recipe first and asks only when it does not clear. After the ask there is one listener, for replies, and one clock, for giving up.
fix: Not built. For a park whose recipe is a re-check of something a person does, keep re-checking on a clock while the question is open, so the act itself is the answer. Then the question can say that no reply is needed.
test: Park a lane the same way, approve inside the wait and write nothing: the run should ship without ending parked, and with no Jev call.

what: The machine cannot tell the owner from an agent that posts as the owner. The shells run under the owner's GitHub account, and so does the machine. Fabrika's builder left a hand-off note on the issue, unmarked, as that account. It was posted before the question, so it was not read. A comment like it posted after a question would be taken for the owner's reply and sent to the Judge, and a sure reading would clear the park on a machine's words.
cause: Whose reply counts is decided by the comment's author, and every writer here has the same author. The hidden-mark rule only covers writers that mark what they post.
fix: Not fixed, by decision. Options: give the shells an account of their own, so the author says who wrote it; have the machine set aside every comment made while one of its shells was running; or count only a reply that names a choice outright.
test: Per lane, list the unmarked comments on the issue by the owner's account and who really wrote each.

what: The merge-queue Listen ran live for the first time. On the second run fabrika's shipper passed every gate, queued the PR, watched the queue for about 8 minutes, and ended its turn with the PR still queued (UNRESOLVED). The PR merged 28 seconds later. The machine was already listening: two reads of the queue 31 seconds apart, the second said landed, and it recorded that on the lane, posted the record, removed the working copy and released the lane. The shipper's 8.7 minutes were an open opus session waiting ($0.29); the machine's wait cost nothing.
fix: Keep the Listen. It is the case for taking the queue wait out of the shipper altogether (experiment 49, item 6): the gates are Checks, the enqueue is an Act, the queue is a Listen.
test: Per lane: minutes the shipper spent watching the queue, and whether the shipper or the machine saw the landing.

what: The field rows called two shippers stopped when each had done what its skill asks: one parked the lane for an approval (AWAITING-CP-APPROVAL), one queued the PR and ran out of watch (UNRESOLVED). Anyone counting stopped shells would have counted two failures that were not.
cause: The row writer knew six terminal words and wrote stopped for any other.
fix: Fixed: AWAITING-CP-APPROVAL is parked, UNRESOLVED is a pass like QUEUED, and the rows for this lane were written with the corrected words.
test: Read each new terminal word a shell reports against the row it produced.

what: The question left no line in the run's printed log. Between the park and the give-up ten minutes later the log shows nothing: not the post, not its link, not the reads of the issue's comments. To find the question I read the run's message file and then the issue.
cause: Only fabrika's verbs are logged as they run. The thread's calls to GitHub go through another Layer with no log hook.
fix: Not built. Log the post with the comment's link, and each reply with its author and whether it was read by code, by Jev, or passed over.
test: After a parked run, find the question's link from the log alone.

what: The ship machine made its first real write. Run as the operator machine's ship stage (SHIP=machine), it read the pull request's facts in 1.2 s, the gate said go, and it put head a150ab9 in the merge queue in 1.8 s: one read and one enqueue call through gh. GitHub dates the queue entry 01:12:57Z, inside the time that Cmd ran. No shipper agent ran. The child stood in reading, enqueueing, queued, finishing and over, and ended done with commit 0da7233. The builder and the reviewer were today's fabrika's agents, and so was the ledger. Run once, on one docs-only pull request with green checks, both reviews passed and no owner's approval needed.
cause: Checked: the run's state lists the child's phases and its outcome, GitHub's events on the pull request show the queue entry and the merge, and no shell was alive from 01:12:51 to the end.
fix: Keep it behind the switch. SHIP=agent stays the default until red checks, an ejection and an approval have each been seen once.
test: Per lane run with SHIP=machine: the child's phases and ending, set beside GitHub's own events on the pull request.

what: The ship machine's own Listen on the merge queue ran live for the first time. It opened right after the enqueue and waited 5.6 minutes with no session open. It said landed about 5 seconds after GitHub's merge time, and named the commit on main, not the head. The ship stage cost $0 and no tokens. A shipper agent doing the same stage cost $0.30 on #559, $0.33 on #625 and $0.29 on #623: a 30,000-token opus session held open for 6 to 9 minutes each time. The whole lane was not cheaper than #559 ($1.73 against $1.74), because its builder and reviewer cost $0.29 more.
cause: Checked against the three earlier lanes' rows in runs.jsonl and the pull request's merge commit on GitHub. The Listen's single reads are not logged, so their count is not known.
fix: Keep the Listen. What it saves is the shipper's session, about 30 cents a lane. The minutes do not change: the queue takes what it takes.
test: Per lane: the ship stage's dollars and minutes, by who ran it, agent or machine.

what: Fabrika took a LANDED line written by the driver when no shipper shell had run. After the child ended done, the operator ran fabrika lane report 561 --task issue --token LANDED --pr with the pull request. Exit 0. Fabrika checked first: its output says the pull request closes the issue on merge and that the issue reads closed. It folded the line as the lane's last event, the next read said complete, and lane record posted the record. That is one of the ten lines the child can write, in the case where everything was true. QUEUED is never written in this mode, so that question was not asked.
cause: Checked in the run's verb log and on the issue. docs/ship-machine.md had listed this as not checked.
fix: Nothing to fix. The other nine lines (ALREADY-MERGED, BASE-CONFLICTED, EJECTED, ROUTED-REPAIR, ROUTED-REVIEW, AWAITING-CP-APPROVAL, REFUSED, UNKNOWN, and the park with no cause) each still need a first real write.
test: Per ship outcome name: the line the driver wrote, fabrika's exit code, and where the lane stood on the next read.

what: The run's own shipper row said minutes 0, and tools 0, for a ship stage that ran about 5.7 minutes (01:12:55 to 01:18:36 UTC). Its note field held a sentence where the schema asks for a note id: the ship machine, no agent: reading > enqueueing > queued > finishing > over; ended done on the pull request. The row in runs.jsonl was put right by hand: minutes 5.7, measured from the run's message file, and note pointing here.
cause: fieldRows in src/operator-host.ts writes minutes 0 and tools 0 as fixed numbers for a stage the ship machine ran. The record the operator keeps of a child (ShipRow in src/turn.ts) holds its phases and its outcome and no time, because a machine reads no clock. So the row writer has nothing to work from.
fix: Not built. The host stamps when a turn enters and leaves shipping, as it already measures the whole run, and hands that to fieldRows. The phases move out of note into a field of their own.
test: After a lane run with SHIP=machine, the shipper row's minutes match the gap between the lane read before ship and the driver's line after it, with no hand edit.

what: The printed log shows nothing from 01:12:56 to 01:18:36, the whole ship stage. A person watching could not see the facts read, the gate's go, the enqueue or the wait on the queue. The one write to GitHub left no line in the verb log either: it shows only as a message type and a phase name. The facts the child read and the gate's answer were not kept anywhere.
cause: Two things. The log prints a line when the run's one-line summary changes, and the summary shows the turn's phase (shipping), not the child's. And only fabrika's verbs are logged as they run: the code host's gh calls go through another Layer with no log hook. The same hole as note 2026-10-11-18.
fix: Not built. Show the child's phase in the summary, log each code host call with its time and how it ended, and keep the facts and the gate's answer beside the run's state.
test: After a lane run with SHIP=machine, say from the log alone when the pull request was queued and what the gate read.

what: In the run's message file ship_facts_ok and ship_enqueue_ok are 7 ms apart, which reads as an enqueue that took 7 ms. It took 1.8 s. The time beside a message is when the Cmds its step sent had finished, not when the message arrived. So ship_facts_ok carries the enqueue's end time, and ship_enqueue_ok, which sends nothing, comes 7 ms later. Nothing was wrong in the run. Anyone timing a Cmd from that file would be wrong.
cause: Checked in tea 0.20.0: the loop saves the state, runs the step's Cmds and waits for them, and only then calls the observers the host stamps from. Checked against the verb log too: start is stamped 2 ms after the claim's last verb.
fix: Not built. Stamp each Cmd's start and end where it is handled, and keep the observer's time under a name that says what it is.
test: For each Cmd in a run, its logged length is within a second of the gap the verb log or GitHub shows.

what: The ship machine shipped a second lane, this time a code change: 11 files in two packages, with a changeset. Run as the operator machine's ship stage (SHIP=machine), it read the pull request's facts in 1.4 s, the gate said go, and it put head 7c2dcc4 in the merge queue in 1.9 s. GitHub dates the queue entry 03:30:03Z, inside the time that Cmd ran. Its Listen waited 7.7 minutes and said landed about 20 seconds after GitHub's merge time, with the commit on main, 9915b2e. The driver wrote LANDED and fabrika took it, exit 0. No shipper agent ran and the stage cost $0. The child stood in reading, enqueueing, queued, finishing and over, and ended done on the pull request. The run's own shipper row again said minutes 0 and held those phases and that ending as a sentence in note, so the row in runs.jsonl was put right by hand as note 2026-10-12-04 describes: minutes 7.7, measured from the run's message file (03:30:00 to 03:37:45 UTC). It is the same straight path as #561: checks green before ship, both reviews passed the first time, no owner's approval needed. The lane was picked in the hope of a failed review and a repair round, so the machine would read a pull request with an old FAIL and a new PASS. The review passed the first time, so that is still not seen. The whole lane cost $3.95 and took 28.3 minutes.
cause: Checked: the run's state lists the child's phases and its outcome, GitHub's events on the pull request show the queue entry at 03:30:03Z and the merge at 03:37:23Z, no shell was alive from 03:29:57 to the end, and neither shell's logged commands name the queue or a merge.
fix: Keep it behind the switch. Two clean lanes on the same path do not change the default. SHIP=agent stays until red checks, an ejection and an approval have each been seen once.
test: Per lane run with SHIP=machine: the child's phases and ending, set beside GitHub's own events on the pull request.

what: The builder waited for the pull request's checks itself, with its session open. It opened the pull request at 03:19:27 UTC and then ran one command that watched the checks until they ended, about 7.5 minutes (03:19:32 to about 03:27:05). So 7.5 of its 17.4 minutes were a wait and about 10 were work. When the driver read the pull request at 03:27:35 every required check had passed, so the driver's own wait on checks never opened and the reviewer started 4 seconds later. On #561 the builder ended right after its push, and the driver's Listen did the same wait for 7.4 minutes with no session open. The lane's clock time is the same either way. What changes is what a builder row's minutes mean: 17.4 beside 4.1 overstates the work, and two builders' minutes compare only with the wait taken out. What the wait cost in dollars is not known: the log keeps one total per shell.
cause: Checked in both builders' shell logs: this one has a gh pr checks --watch call after its push, the #561 one has none. Fabrika's build skill leaves it to the builder: it says how to wait if the builder waits on the checks before it hands off, and does not say whether to. The wait ran as a normal command, not in the background, so the shell reported at its end, unlike the three builders of note 2026-10-11-08.
fix: Not built. Under the machine, tell the builder to end once the pull request is open and leave the wait to the driver's Listen, which is already there and holds no session. What that gives up: a builder that waits can mend a red check in the same session, and without it a red check comes back through a reviewer first (note 2026-10-11-10). Until then, take the wait out by hand when comparing builder rows.
test: Per builder shell under the machine: the minutes between its push and its last word. It should be under one.

what: tea-fabrika's first review piece (src/stages/review/) was run alone on heads today's reviewer had already reviewed. It only read, and posted nothing. On the first head of #625 its gate read the required check as red and answered send:builder:checks_red in 2.4 seconds, with no agent, for $0. Today's reviewer on that head took 131 seconds and $1.00 to reach the same answer: FAIL on both kinds, for the red check. But today's reviewer also opened the failing log, named the test and guessed the cause, and the repair went after that guess. The piece says only that the check is red, and which one. On the final head of #625 one reviewer agent with three read tools filled a form: 5 rows, all pass, each with a limit, and no finding. Code made that a pass for both kinds, the same as today's reviewer, for $0.90 against $0.87. A small probe on a made-up brief (another model, low effort, $0.11) showed the agent had its three read tools and the one tool that hands the answer back, that a read outside its folder was refused, and that a criterion whose proof is in the pull request's text came back unseen. With the run in note 2026-10-12-10, four runs cost $2.13. Three heads show the plumbing works. They do not measure agreement.
cause: Checked: each run's saved file holds the pack, the sheet, the verdicts and the spend, and today's verdicts on the same heads are public comments. Not checked: whether a second run on one head gives the same rows.
fix: Built as a first piece: a Check before the reviewer that sends a red head back with no agent. Not built: saying why the check is red (step 11 in docs/review-machine.md), which today's reviewer did and the repair used.
test: On recorded lanes: every head with a red required check ends send:builder:checks_red with no agent started, and the builder that gets it needs no more repair rounds than after today's verdict.

what: On the head of #622 that today's reviewer passed, tea-fabrika's review piece (run alone, read only, nothing posted) answered send:builder:review_failed. Two things, and only the second is surely a fault. First, one row apart: criterion 7 says the output names every removed subpath. Both reviewers saw the same fact, that a removed subpath which published no name is not named. The builder had declared that as a deviation and filed an issue for it. Today's reviewer graded the row PASS with a named limit. The piece's reviewer graded it fail and wrote one finding, code-af348b55, with the lines, the proof and what it wants. Nobody has judged which grade is right. Second, the doc kind failed too, and its printed comment says fail above a list of what has to change that reads Nothing. That is the piece's own rule: a row belongs to no kind, so one failed row fails every kind the change owes, and each comment repeats all 11 rows. Today's doc verdict grades only the criteria its kind carries. The run cost $1.12 and 2.6 minutes, against $1.01 and 2.3 for today's reviewer.
cause: Checked for the second: src/stages/review/verdict.ts fails a kind on any failed row. For the first, as far as checked: the piece's reviewer is given the rubric texts but not the review skill's own rules, and nothing in its prompt says how a declared deviation changes a row's grade. Whether that is why the two grades differ is a guess.
fix: Not built. Decide how a declared deviation changes a row's grade and put the rule where code applies it, not in the reviewer's head. Decide whether a row belongs to a kind, so a doc review does not fail on a code row.
test: Replay the recorded heads where a builder declared a gap in a criterion: the row's grade is the same on every run and matches the rule. And no printed comment says fail with nothing to change.

what: One operator carried #631 from a ruled ticket to a merged pull request in 45 minutes with no park and no person. It started five shells: builder, reviewer, builder, reviewer, shipper. The shells' own time adds up to 41.1 minutes: build 13.1, review 19.2, ship 8.8. The operator's own time between stages was 10 to 30 seconds each. To decide what comes next five times and write the ledger, the operator made 48 tool calls and its conversation grew to 141,311 tokens, about the size of the first builder's (145,876) and more than either reviewer's.
cause: Checked: times, tool calls and sizes are read from each run's saved transcript, and the stage times match the operator's own report.
fix: A machine holds the loop. The five starts and the ledger writes become Cmds, and no conversation grows while the shells work.
test: Drive a lane of the same shape (one review fail, one repair, a queue wait) with the operator machine and compare the driver's tokens and Cmds with 141,311 tokens and 48 tool calls.

what: The shipper put the pull request in the merge queue and watched for its full window, 480 seconds and 16 polls. The merge landed about 6 seconds before the window closed, and the shipper still returned unresolved. The ledger then said the lane was queued while the change was already on main. One more queue read by the operator set it right. Because the shipper's watch ended first, its release step and its own cleanup did not run. Its report also told the driver to run a recover verb, where the operator's skill names a different pair of verbs for the same case.
cause: Checked from the operator's report and the merge time on the pull request. Not checked: why the last poll missed a merge that was 6 seconds old.
fix: The ship stage listens for the merge as an event with no window of its own. A shell that times out cannot leave the ledger behind the truth, because no shell holds the wait.
test: On recorded lanes: count ship stages whose recorded outcome was unresolved while the pull request was already merged. The machine's ship stage should have none.

what: The one review fail named no criterion on the ticket. All eight rows passed. The reviewer found that three texts (a doc comment, the changeset, the generated reference page) said a library call keeps the checks of a schema that needs a service. It ran the call on the pinned library version and the checks were dropped. It added a ninth row to the ticket's criteria and graded the repair against that row. The repair changed three files and no code, and cost one of three retries and about 12 minutes of build and review. The builder had written the sentence on its own: neither the ticket nor the ruling says what happens to such a schema.
cause: Checked: both verdict comments and the repair commit are public. The reviewer's measurement is in its verdict.
fix: Keep this move. A reviewer may test a claim the change makes about the outside world and add a row for it. In tea-fabrika's review piece a row comes only from the ticket today, so this finding would have no row to sit on.
test: Replay this head through the review piece: it should end with a failed row that names the three texts. Today it has no way to add a row.

what: The builder's own pre-push check came back red in both rounds, on one guard only (the code-owners guard). Both times the builder judged it a known false red and pushed anyway. It was right. But the only thing between a real red and a push was the builder remembering which red is safe to ignore.
cause: Checked: the false red is a filed bug in both repos. Not checked: how the builder knew, from the skill text or from the tickets.
fix: A gate's answer is a typed value with a reason, and the list of reds that do not block lives in code next to the gate. A builder never decides whether a red check counts.
test: On recorded lanes: count pushes made past a red pre-push check, and for each whether the red was on the known-safe list.

what: Small things the lane worked around or left behind. The pinned CLI has no verbs for a lane's working copy, cleanup or leave, and no verb for a builder to read comments, so three working copies stayed on disk and the builder read the ruling through raw API calls. The record step could not sync its table because no table project exists, and every brief said there was no size to stop at. The brief has no field for a ruling, so the ruling reached the builder only through the ticket's thread. The harness refused three commands that named the main checkout, though none of them ran git. The workspace CLI, run from a working copy, warned that it was the global install, which it was not. A review post was refused twice until the evidence row repeated a source phrase word for word; a link to the same comment was not enough. The closed ticket still carries its triaged and ready-for-agent labels.
cause: Checked from the operator's report. Each item is as the operator or a shell reported it; none was re-run.
fix: Each of these is an Act with a typed answer in the machine: cleanup is a Cmd that runs at the end of every lane, a ruling is a field of the brief, and evidence points at a comment by its id, not by matching words.
test: On recorded lanes: count working copies left after a lane ends, and review posts refused for wording when the link was right.

what: The session that started the operator was told the operator had finished while the operator's shipper was still running. The operator's turn had only ended to wait; it was woken again when the shipper returned and then finished the lane properly. The driving session read the first notice as the operator giving up, and reported that to a person as a dropped hand-over. That was wrong and was corrected. Inside the lane the same doubling showed up: each of the five shells' results reached the operator twice, once as the report and once as a notice that the report had arrived.
cause: Checked: the first notice came before the merge, the second after, and the operator's final report covers the shipper's outcome. Not checked: whether a notice that says finished can be told apart from one that says waiting.
fix: A finished lane is one typed outcome from the machine. Waiting is a state the machine is in, not a message, so a driver cannot mistake it for an end.
test: With the operator machine driving a lane, the driver receives exactly one end outcome per lane and one result per shell.

what: Five triagers ran side by side on the whole untriaged list, one ticket each. All five were back in under 7 minutes: two triaged for an agent, one triaged and waiting on a ruling, one parked on a question, one closed as not planned. Four of them ran the reported case before pricing it, and three corrected the report: one bug was wider than filed, one claim in a feature request was wrong and made the work smaller, and one gate named in a bug report could not crash the way the report said. Each run grew to between 90,000 and 118,000 tokens to do it.
cause: Checked: outcomes are read back from the tickets; sizes and times from each run's saved transcript.
fix: Keep the move: reproduce before pricing. In a machine the reproduction is its own step with a typed result (reproduced, not reproduced, could not run), so a ticket cannot be priced on a claim nobody ran.
test: On recorded triage runs: the share of tickets priced after a reproduction ran, and how many reports were corrected by it.

what: A small bug in one package was parked for a person because the triager found no place it was allowed to go: every milestone for that package is a running campaign, and the rule says a running campaign takes no new low-priority work. Two tickets of the same package and the same priority were put on that same milestone two days earlier, by triagers reading the same rule. Same rule, opposite call. The triager also said it was only about 55 percent sure the park was what the owner would want.
cause: Checked: the two earlier tickets carry that milestone, and this one was parked with the reason in a comment. Not checked: why the earlier triagers read the rule the other way.
fix: Where a ticket may live is a gate in code that reads the roadmap and answers with a typed value. Two tickets with the same facts get the same answer, and the case with no legal home shows up once, as a gap in the roadmap, not once per ticket.
test: Replay the recorded triage runs through the gate: tickets with the same package, priority and roadmap state get the same home.

what: Three of the five triagers found something new on the way and had nowhere to put it. One, while closing a ticket as not planned, saw that a published stylesheet path marked stable is outside the check that guards removals; it wrote that into the close comment of the closed ticket. The driver read the report, checked the source and filed it as its own ticket. One found two more ways the same tool exits with the wrong code and left them in the ticket body as out of scope. One noticed that a sibling ticket looked like a duplicate of an older one and could only mention it. A triager's claim covers one ticket, and its outcome has no slot for a finding about anything else.
cause: Checked: the close comment, the new ticket and the reports. The skill's rule that a claim covers one ticket is as the triagers stated it.
fix: A stage's outcome carries a list of findings beside its verdict. The machine files each one as a report, so a finding is never left in a comment on a closed ticket.
test: On recorded runs: count findings written into a body or a comment that were never filed. With the typed outcome that count is zero.

what: Places where the triage skill and the pinned CLI disagree. The skill's last step calls a verb the CLI does not have; four of five triagers hit it and each decided alone that skipping was safe. The verb that says whether a ticket can be built answers eligible for a ticket parked for a person, because it reads only dependency edges. The skill and the guard ask for two different texts for the same pitch approval, and the triager could not tell which one is accepted. A scratch file for a reproduction cannot have a file ending, so one triager type-checked its cases in memory and kept no file.
cause: Checked from the four reports, each with the exact message. None re-run.
fix: The steps live in the machine, so there is no skill text that can name a verb the code does not have. An approval is a typed value, not a line of text two readers parse differently.
test: Count shell reports that say a step was skipped because a verb was missing. A machine-driven triage has none.

what: For the second lane in a row the shipper's watch on the merge queue ended as unresolved right as the merge landed. The shipper reported it had not seen the merge, and the operator had to look at the pull request itself to learn the lane was done. Two lanes today, two times. The same thing is in note 2026-10-13-02.
cause: Checked: both shipper reports and both merge times. Not checked: whether the watch has a fixed window that happens to match how long the queue takes here.
fix: The merge is an event the machine listens for, with no window that can close first. The ship stage ends on the event, and a wait that runs out is its own typed outcome, never the same word as a merge that failed.
test: Replay the two recorded ship stages against the queue's event times: the stage ends as merged both times.

what: A change passed build and review while one line of its ruling may not hold. The ruling says nothing is saved after the stop call has returned. The builder that repaired the pull request read the code and saw a path where a store call the stop had given up on can still save, or start a subscription, later. It filed a new ticket for it. The review passed on the same head, and the merged decision record states the promise as kept. The case was read from code and not run. It reached the board only because one builder chose to file it.
cause: Checked: the ruling line, the new ticket, the review verdict. Not checked: the case itself; a triager was asked to run it.
fix: Each ruled line becomes a row the review must answer with a run, not with a read. A stage's outcome carries a list of findings beside its verdict, and the machine files each one, so a known gap cannot ride along with a pass.
test: Replay this head through a review that needs one run per ruled line: the row for the save after the stop call comes back as not shown.

what: The builder made three calls the ruling does not cover and wrote them down only in its report. The stop call waits twice, each wait with the same time limit, so the worst case is twice the limit. The last save has no time limit at all. A caller's send that sits in line behind a handler that never returns is never answered. None of the three was put to the person who ruled, and none is in the ticket.
cause: Checked: the builder's report. Not checked: the three behaviors in the merged code.
fix: A builder that meets a point the ruling is silent on returns a typed open question. The machine then either asks the person or records the call as the builder's own, in the ticket, where the reviewer reads it.
test: On recorded build runs: count calls made outside the ruling that appear only in a report. With the typed question that count is zero.

what: The one review fail of the lane was about four sentences in doc comments that a point of the ruling asks for. The repair changed comments only. That round took a second builder run and a second review run: about 11 minutes and about 228 thousand tokens, for four sentences. Neither reviewer ran the tests itself; both read the results of the checks on the pull request.
cause: Checked: the two verdicts, the repair's diff as the operator described it, and the run stats.
fix: Before the hand-over, the build stage checks its own change against each ruled point as a list. A missing doc sentence is caught in the build run, at the price of one more turn there, not a full round.
test: Replay the first head through that list: the four missing sentences are named before any reviewer starts.

what: Two reports were written from a read of the code, with no run. Each triager was asked to run the case before it set a price, and the run changed the answer both times. For the first, filed by the driver, the main claim was wrong: the check it named does skip the path, but a test that runs on every pull request catches the removal, so nothing would merge. It was closed. For the second, filed by a builder, one of three claims held when run, one was a weaker thing than claimed, and one was wrong. Each run took about five minutes.
cause: Checked: both triage reports with their run tables, and the labels read back from the board.
fix: A report that names a behavior carries a run, or the triage stage runs it before any price is set. A claim read from code is typed as not run, so no later stage can take it for a fact.
test: On recorded reports that were read from code only: run each one and count how many change their answer. Here it was two of two.

what: Follow-up to note 2026-10-13-12, now with a run. The merged change breaks one line of its ruling in one case. The ruling says nothing is saved after the stop call has returned. In three runs out of three, with the store's load held past the time limit, the stop call returned, the load then came back, and the engine started a new save. Two reviews had passed that head, and the merged decision record repeats the ruled line with no exception. A second case is weaker: a save that was already running when the stop call gave up can still finish late, and the record's sentence does not allow for that either. The claim about subscriptions starting late did not hold.
cause: Checked: the triager's run log on the main branch at the merge commit, three rounds. Not checked: the second engine, which shares the same loop.
fix: Each ruled line is a row the review answers with a run of its own, including the slow-store case, not with a read of the diff. A row with no run comes back as not shown, and not shown does not pass.
test: Replay the merged head through a review with one run per ruled line: the row for a save after the stop call fails on the held-load case.

what: The triager found that one ruled sentence promises more than the engine can do: a store call that is already running cannot be called back. It wrote criteria that narrow the sentence in the decision record, and sent the ticket to an agent, not to the person who ruled. It said it was about 75 percent sure of that choice. It also left one new choice to the builder with no ruling behind it: whether a run whose first save was dropped starts or fails. Triage has no way to say this needs one small answer from the person and nothing else; its only choices are an agent or a full park.
cause: Checked: the triager's report and the rewritten ticket body.
fix: A change to the words of a ruled line is a typed question to the person who ruled, raised by the machine, while the rest of the ticket stays ready. The builder never gets to narrow a ruling by writing the record.
test: On recorded tickets whose criteria edit a ruled line: each one raises exactly one question to the person before a build starts.

what: A second ruled line that the merged stop change does not keep, found by a throwaway run after the merge and not by the lane. The decision record says a message dropped when the stop call gives up is reported, never silent. In the run, 20 messages waited behind a handler that never returns: none was folded, none of the 20 sends ever got an answer, and the stop notice named the stuck handler but had no field for the messages in line. With a handler that returns late, each send did get an error, but only the code holding that send saw it. The next epic had a criterion that asked a test to pin what the stop error names; as written, a builder could have passed it by pinning the silence. The criterion was rewritten before any plan was made.
cause: Checked: the run record, three passes per case on both engines, and the rewritten criterion. Not checked: why two reviews of the lane did not catch it.
fix: A criterion that says pin what happens is rewritten at plan time into the outcome the ruling asks for, with a named run. The plan check refuses a row that any behavior at all would pass.
test: Run the plan check over the epic's first criteria list: the row about the stop error is refused as passable by today's behavior.

what: A lane whose whole job was to write down a ruling that already existed: one decision record and one row in an index, no code. It ran clean, one round per stage, no park, merged in about 26 minutes. It still took four agents and about 370 thousand tokens. The review took longer than the build, and most of that was a wait for one check on a change with no code in it. The ship stage saw the merge land this time, the first of three lanes today.
cause: Checked: the operator's stage table and the merged pull request. Shell token counts are the operator's rounded figures.
fix: A record written from a ruling is one draft and one check of the draft against the ruling's lines, driven by the machine. No driver agent, and no wait on code checks for a change that touches no code.
test: Replay this lane as draft plus check: same two files, and compare minutes and tokens with the 26 minutes and 370 thousand here.

what: Two calls the builder made alone, both disclosed in the pull request and both merged with no one answering them. Its own pre-push check came back red on a guard that wants owner rows for paths this repository does not have; it judged the guard unrelated to its two files and pushed. The reviewer took that at its word and did not run the guard. The builder also wrote into the record which two published entries the new helper ships from, a name the ruling does not spell out, and marked it as needing a yes. The lane has no step where that yes can be given, so the record merged with the name in it.
cause: Checked: the operator's report of the builder's and the reviewer's words. Not checked: the raw text of the red check.
fix: A deviation a builder declares is a typed open question on the lane, not a paragraph in the pull request. The machine routes it: a guard that does not apply to this repository is settled once in config, and a name the ruling left open goes to the person who ruled before the merge.
test: On recorded pull requests with a deviations section: each entry has an answer on record before the merge. Here it is zero of two.

what: The skills in use are newer than the pinned command line tool, and every run today paid for it. Four verbs the skills call do not exist in the tool: three for making and removing a lane's working copy and one for reading a ticket's comments. So no run cleaned up after itself; working copies from three lanes and two triage runs are still on disk. A builder read its ruling through another verb that flattens line breaks. The tool also warned that it was a global install when it was the pinned one, and the harness refused two plain shell lines from an isolated agent as too complex to check.
cause: Checked: the exact messages in five reports, and the list of working copies on disk.
fix: Steps live in the machine's code, so a step and the tool it calls are one version. Cleaning up a working copy is the last Cmd of a lane, with its own result, not a line of skill text an agent may find missing.
test: After a machine-driven lane ends, list the working copies on disk: none belongs to that lane.

what: The pitch approval for an epic is a one-line comment, and the skill text says an agent never posts it. The driver told the owner he had to type it himself. He told the driver to post it for him, and it went out from his account. Nothing in the tool can tell the two cases apart: the check reads a comment from an allowed account, not who typed it. The rule held for a few hours as a line of text, and its only effect was one more round trip with the owner.
cause: Checked: the comment on the epic and the skill's wording.
fix: An approval is an answer to a typed question the machine asks the person, in the place the person already is. The record is the answer event, with the question it answers, not a comment whose text a reader has to parse.
test: Count the round trips between asking for an approval and having it on record. Here it was two; with a typed question it is one.

what: Planning the epic took the driver about nine minutes of tool time once the brief was good: one claim, one staged plan, six child tickets, the order, the edges. Most of the thinking had been done before, in the brief and its checks. Two things stood out. The rule that every epic is grilled was met with two fact questions the planner asked and answered itself; one of them did change the plan (the list of files the removal touches was five files short). And three calls the planner made (split the first step in two, add a last slice for the end-to-end test and docs, run all six in a strict line) are the planner's alone by the skill's rules, and reach the owner only as lines in a read-back before he approves.
cause: Checked: the verbs' answers and the epic body. The planner's token use was not measured; it ran in the driver's own session.
fix: The plan is a typed value: stories, slices, edges, each slice's criteria. A draft step fills it from the brief and a check step runs every rule the plan gate runs, before anything is created on the board. Shape choices are fields with a reason, so the read-back to the owner is generated, not written by hand.
test: Feed the same brief to the draft step twice: the same slices and edges come out, and the gate's checks pass before the first ticket exists.

what: Third time in four lanes today that the shipper's watch ended as unresolved within seconds of the merge. The watch ran its whole window of 480 seconds, the pull request merged right as it closed, and the operator learned of the merge from its own single read a moment later. The shipper then skipped its last step because it never saw the landing. The one lane where the watch did see the merge was the one with no code checks to wait for.
cause: Checked: four shipper reports and the merge times. The window length is the tool's own number as the shipper printed it; the queue's usual time here was not measured.
fix: Same as note 2026-10-13-11: the merge is an event the machine listens for, with no window sized by guess. With four data points the window and the queue time look like the same length, which is the worst possible setting.
test: Replay the four ship stages against the queue's event times: all four end as merged, and the last step runs in all four.

what: A change in behavior that nobody ruled on merged, although every stage saw it. To make its test pass on one engine, the builder made the stop call run its shutdown only once, so a second stop call no longer runs the last save again. The ruling for the ticket does not name this. The builder wrote it into the pull request, the reviewer flagged it in both of its verdicts and passed anyway, the operator noted it and went on to ship, and the queue merged it. Two smaller calls went the same way. This is the third lane today where a builder's own call outside the ruling reached the main branch with no answer from the person who ruled; here the brief had told every shell to say so and not settle it, and they did say so. Saying so stopped nothing.
cause: Checked: the operator's report with the verdict links. Not checked: the changed behavior itself.
fix: A declared deviation is a typed open question that holds the lane. The review stage cannot pass while one is open; it comes back as needs an answer, and the machine takes the one question to the person. Text in a pull request holds nothing.
test: Replay this lane with the deviation as a typed question: the review ends as needs an answer, and the ship stage never starts.

what: Three things about how this review got its facts. The owner's ruling for the ticket was a plain comment, and the verb that hands a reviewer its criteria and rulings reported zero rulings, because the comment had no marker. The reviewer graded against it only because the driver had pointed at it by hand. The reviewer ran the new tests itself three times, which the repository's own rules ask for and the review skill forbids (it says never check out the head); it followed the repository. And the one check that would show the tests fail without the fix, its own probe, was refused by the harness as too complex a shell line, so it never ran.
cause: Checked: the operator's report of the reviewer's words and the exact refusal text.
fix: A ruling is a typed value attached to the ticket, so every stage gets it without a marker in prose. Running the new tests, and running them once with the fix taken out, are Check steps the machine owns; the reviewer agent judges what the checks cannot.
test: For a ticket ruled in a plain comment: the review stage's input lists the ruling. For a fix: the check run with the fix removed fails, and that result is on record.

what: The plan gate for a six-child epic ran as a fresh agent, because the planner may not gate its own plan. It took 24 tool calls, about 86 thousand tokens and under three minutes. Every pass or fail answer came from seven verbs run in a fixed order (claim, read, approval, check, flip, verdict, release); none refused. The agent's own judgment added only six advisory notes to the verdict, and to write them it read the issue bodies outside any verb, since the read verb prints counts and not the criteria text. The notes change nothing: two say a child is too broad for one pull request, which is the planner's own named doubt, and the gate passed and flipped all six children anyway. One skill example carries a fixed digest that does not belong to this epic; the agent used the one the check returned.
cause: Checked: the agent's report with each verb's answer and exit code, and the labels read back after the run.
fix: The seven verbs in a fixed order are a Check the machine runs with no agent. The advisory read is a separate Judge step with the child bodies as typed input, and a note that says a child is too broad becomes a typed answer the machine can act on (hold that child, ask) and not a line in a comment.
test: Run the gate as a machine on this epic: same verdict and the same six flips with zero agent tokens. Feed it a child flagged too broad: the machine holds that child and asks.

what: First lane today where a builder's own calls outside the ruling did not reach review or the main branch unanswered. On the second child of a six-child epic the builder listed seven choices neither the ruling nor the ticket covers (which form of the machine definition gets port types, whether a handler's follow-up message is checked on the way in, three extra refusals when a machine is defined, what the test harness checks, how one criterion word was read, two additions to error types). The operator read the list, stopped the child before its review and wrote the questions as one note for the owner. It cost 73 minutes of lane time to get there and the lane now waits on a person. The pipeline gave no help: the pinned tool has no park reason for an owed ruling (the flag was refused, so the park carries no cause), its unpark verb refuses a park with no cause, and the skill names no route for this case. The operator chose to park before review, so no review time is spent on code that may change, and no reviewer findings exist yet for that child.
cause: Checked: the operator's report, the builder's list on the ticket, the park note on the epic. Not checked: the seven choices against the code.
fix: A builder's Draft ends with a typed list of open questions next to the code. A non-empty list is its own outcome: the machine holds the child and takes the questions to the person, one at a time. The operator did this by reading prose; the machine does it from the type.
test: Replay this child: the build ends as needs an answer with seven typed questions, review does not start, and the lane resumes from review when each has an answer.

what: The driver's two instructions for builders (where the ruling is, and do not settle a point it is silent on) never reached a builder. The operator posted them as comments on each child ticket, the one channel the skill allows. The pinned tool has no verb for a builder to read a ticket's comments, so each builder read the ticket body only. The second builder found the ruling by itself in the decision record and still settled seven open points; it did declare them. Also on this lane: the build check ended with the same refusal in all three builder runs (a guard that wants owner rows for paths this repository does not have), and every builder committed past it and said so. One builder used a replace script once against the edit-tool rule and reported it.
cause: Checked: the operator's report and the builders' own disclosures. Not checked: the builders' transcripts.
fix: What a builder must know is its typed input, gathered by the machine before the builder starts: the ticket, the rulings that bind it, and the driver's standing rules. Nothing depends on a builder going to look for a comment. A guard that fails the same way on every run is fixed or switched off in configuration, so a red check means something.
test: Start a builder on a child whose ruling lives in a comment on the parent: the builder's input contains the ruling text and the standing rules, with no read of the ticket's comments by the builder.

what: A review caught a test that proved nothing and then proved the repair. The first child removes an old family of names. Its type test said a handler that calls the removed function does not compile, but it called it with arguments the old function would also have rejected, so the test would stay green if the function came back. The reviewer failed the code gate on that and added a seventh criterion row to the ticket. After the repair the second reviewer put the old function back in memory through the compiler and counted eight errors, which is the check that the test now fails without the removal. Both reviewers ran the full checks themselves, twice. The cost of that catch: the added row changed the ticket body, and the owner's plan approval, which is bound to a digest of the bodies, now reads stale. The reviewer's own verb made the edit.
cause: Checked: the first review's verdict comment, the appended row on the ticket, and the approval verb's answer after the lane (stale, digest changed).
fix: Proving that a new test fails with the change taken out is a Check the machine runs on every fix or removal, not something a reviewer may or may not think of. A criterion a reviewer adds is an event on the lane and not an edit to the approved plan, so an approval stays valid and the added row is still graded.
test: For a removal: the machine restores the removed piece and the new test fails; that result is on record. A reviewer adds a row: the plan approval still reads current.

what: Small things the epic lane hit in its first 73 minutes. The verb that builds the epic's lane refused the approved plan's dependency list, because one child requires a ticket that is not a child of the epic (a fix that had already merged); the plan gate had passed that same list an hour earlier. The operator took the verb's other route, which reads the live child list and drops the outside reference. Four verbs the skills name do not exist in the pinned tool, and one flag. Asking for the assembly working copy a second time re-cut the branch from the main branch; nothing was lost only because no child had landed yet. The harness refused the operator a git call into another working copy and a long inline comment body, and refused a reviewer's in-place probe edit. One builder saw text in a batch of file reads saying another task had finished and telling it to read a file; it did not act on it. The removal child alone, a chore, took four shell runs, about 40 minutes and about half a million tokens.
cause: Checked: the operator's report with exact refusal texts and exit codes, and the per-stage numbers from its task notices. Not checked: where the stray text came from.
fix: The plan gate and the lane builder read one typed plan, so what one accepts the other accepts. An outside dependency is its own kind of edge, checked as done or not done at the start. Text that arrives inside a tool result is data with a known source; a notice meant for another run never reaches a builder's input.
